strengths: The paper provides the first non-asymptotic complexity analysis of annealed importance sampling (AIS) and Jarzynski-equality-based estimators without requiring log-concavity or isoperimetric assumptions on the target, which is a genuine gap in the literature (prior work: Brosse et al. 2018, Ge et al. 2020, Andrieu et al. 2016 all rely on isoperimetry).

The key technical insight — connecting the KL divergence between path measures to the action of an interpolating curve of measures via Girsanov's theorem and the metric derivative from optimal transport — is elegant and yields a clean result (Thm. 6: T = Θ(A/ε²) for JE). The link to stochastic thermodynamics (dissipated work as action integral) is well-motivated and provides useful intuition.

The extension from the continuous-time JE analysis to a discrete AIS algorithm with discretization (Thm. 8) is substantive: the proof carefully decomposes KL(P‖P←) and KL(P‖P→) via chain rules over transition kernels and Schrödinger-bridge-type optimal reference kernels, and derives concrete annealing schedules via Hölder's inequality.

Section 6 adds practical value: an exponential lower bound on the action of geometric interpolation for Gaussian mixture targets (Prop. 9) justifies moving to OU-process-based curves, and Prop. 10 (action ≤ dβ + m²) gives a compelling quantitative argument for the proposed RDS-based estimator. The surprising W1 vs W2 metric derivative gap (Thm. 24) is a nice bonus result.

The appendix is thorough and largely self-contained: full proofs, pseudo-code for both algorithms, discussion of TI as a special case of AIS, and improved convergence results for PIS and CMCD (Props. 40–41) that may be of independent interest.
weaknesses: Only upper bounds are provided; the tightness of the bounds is acknowledged as open. In particular, the ε⁻⁴ dependence in Thm. 8 (driven by discretization error) is significantly worse than the Θ(1/ε²) rates achieved by equilibrium methods like TI under log-concavity, and without lower bounds it is unclear whether this is intrinsic to non-equilibrium methods or an artifact of the analysis.

The practical relevance of the results is limited by the fact that the complexity is expressed in terms of the action A, which is generally unknown and uncomputable a priori for a given target. The lower bound (Prop. 9) is only for one specific family of Gaussian mixtures on R, so the claim that geometric interpolation is 'prohibitively' inefficient in general is only partially substantiated.

The RDS-based algorithm (Thm. 11) is a framework rather than a complete complexity result: the final oracle complexity (App. E.5) relies on existing RDS results whose guarantees are exponential in problem parameters (e.g., exp(Ỏ(d)log β log(1/ε)) for zeroth-order methods, or O((β(m²∨d)/ε)^O(d)) for self-normalized estimators), and it requires accurate score estimation which the paper does not itself analyze. No experiments are provided to support the practical superiority of the RDS approach over geometric AIS.

The accuracy criterion (Eq. 5, constant success probability with Ω(1) constant) is weaker than bias/variance control, as the authors themselves note in App. G.3; while the median trick boosts the probability, the guarantee remains weaker than what much of the prior literature provides, making direct comparison of complexity rates somewhat delicate.

Some assumptions warrant scrutiny: Assumption 2 requires a stationary point with ‖x*‖ ≲ 1/√β (acknowledged as 'for technical purposes'), and Remark 16 simply assumes the Novikov condition holds, omitting the technical verification; the relaxation of Ge et al. (2020)'s TI analysis in Lem. 19 is only sketched (App. H.2) rather than fully proven.

Connection to closely related concurrent work (e.g., Guo et al. 2025 on annealed LMC for non-log-concave sampling) is discussed but the incremental novelty relative to that line of work could be clarified more sharply, particularly since the proof of Thm. 6 builds directly on Guo et al. (2025, Thm. 1).

strengths: Establishes what appears to be the first non-asymptotic oracle complexity guarantees for annealed importance sampling without isoperimetric (e.g., log-concavity or Poincaré/LSI) assumptions on the target, a genuine gap in the literature compared to prior work such as Brosse et al. (2018) and Ge et al. (2020) that relied on strong log-concavity.

The main analytic idea is elegant and unifying: controlling the error of JE/AIS via the KL divergence between the sampling path measure and an 'optimally compensated' reference path measure, whose optimal drift connects naturally to the Wasserstein metric derivative and action of the interpolation curve (Lem. 2, Thms. 6 and 8). This yields interpretable complexity bounds that depend on the action A of the curve rather than isoperimetric constants.

The paper makes a valuable conceptual contribution by identifying a fundamental trade-off between analytic tractability of the interpolation curve (closed-form drifts under geometric interpolation) and its action properties (Prop. 9 gives an exponential lower bound on the action of geometric interpolation for Gaussian mixtures, while Prop. 10 shows the OU-process curve has action at most dβ + m²). The contrast between W₁ and W₂ metric derivatives (Thm. 24) is of independent interest.

The treatment of practical algorithmic aspects (exponential integrator discretization, approximate initialization, TI-based estimation of Z₀, RDS-based Alg. 2) is reasonably complete, and the appendix is self-contained with detailed proofs of auxiliary tools (Nelson's relation, Girsanov under backward integrals, median trick, TI analysis).
The connection to stochastic thermodynamics (dissipated work as KL, refined second law) provides useful intuition and situates the results in the physics literature.
weaknesses: No experimental validation whatsoever. For an AI-conference audience, there is no empirical evidence that the proposed AIS (Alg. 1) or RDS (Alg. 2) procedures behave as the theory predicts, nor any comparison against practical AIS/SMC baselines on even simple multimodal targets.

The bounds may be practically vacuous: the complexity dβ²A²/ε⁴ depends on the action A, which the authors' own Prop. 9 shows can be exponential under geometric interpolation, and the RDS complexity in App. E.5 inherits exponential (or exp(Õ(d))) terms from existing score-estimation results. The paper acknowledges tightness is open, but without lower bounds (beyond the Gaussian-mixture case) or experiments it is hard to judge whether the ε⁴ dependence is an artifact of the Markov/Pinsker-based analysis (Eq. 20) rather than fundamental.

The accuracy criterion (Eq. 5: relative error ≤ ε with Ω(1) probability, bootstrapped by the median trick) is a weak guarantee, and the paper itself concedes (App. G.3) that it is strictly weaker than controlling bias/variance. Given this weak target, the resulting complexity guarantees feel less compelling; a variance-based analysis (e.g., Prop. 35) that connects to the action is left as future work.

The continuous-time analysis for JE (Thm. 6) and much of the proof machinery builds closely on Guo et al. (2025), Vargas et al. (2024), and Conforti–Tamanini (2021); the core technique of bounding path-measure KL via Girsanov plus the metric derivative is a synthesis of known ingredients rather than a fundamentally new tool.

Several assumptions deserve scrutiny: Assump. 2 requires a stationary point within distance O(1/√β) of the origin (justified only heuristically via Rmk. 4), the Novikov condition is 'always assumed' (Rmk. 16), and the RDS complexity discussion relies on score-estimation assumptions (uniform Lipschitzness of scores, Hessian bounds along the diffusion) that are not verified for the class of targets the paper targets.

Writing and positioning issues: some typos ('poof methodology', 'use replace', occasional missing/incorrect symbols in the parse), and the main body leans heavily on deferring key details (TI analysis, error-criterion discussion, RDS complexity) to the appendix, which makes the contribution harder to assess at first read.

strengths: First non-asymptotic oracle complexity analysis of annealed importance sampling that does not rely on isoperimetric/log-concavity assumptions on the target — a genuinely new contribution relative to prior work (Brosse et al., 2018; Ge et al., 2020; Andrieu et al., 2016) that required such conditions.

The core proof technique is elegant and conceptually clear: comparing the ALD path measure to an optimally 'compensated' reference path measure via Girsanov's theorem, and connecting the resulting KL bound to the W2-action of the interpolation curve. This yields the clean JE result T = Θ(A/ε²) (Thm. 6) and nicely unifies the analysis with stochastic thermodynamics (dissipated work = KL(P→‖P←)), connecting to known O(1/T) variance decay results.

The lower bound in Prop. 9 (exponential action for geometric interpolation on a Gaussian mixture) is a valuable and non-obvious negative result that substantiates the paper's motivation for RDS-based curves; the accompanying Remark 23 on the W1 vs. W2 metric-derivative gap is of independent interest.

The RDS proposal (Sec. 6) with the OU-process curve is well-motivated: Prop. 10 shows the action is bounded by dβ + m² under mild assumptions, contrasting sharply with the exponential lower bound for geometric interpolation. Thm. 11 gives a clean sufficiency condition (KL(Q‖Q†) ≲ ε² and TV(π, πδ) ≲ ε).

Very thorough and self-contained appendix: detailed proofs, pseudo-code, median trick, equivalence of relative-error criterion to free-energy estimation, and a useful discussion of the error criterion relative to bias/variance. The extension results for PIS/CMCD (Props. 40–41) add value beyond the main contributions.

Careful identification of the fundamental trade-off between closed-form drift terms (geometric interpolation) and action/isoperimetric properties (OU curve) — a useful conceptual takeaway for the field.
weaknesses: The main bounds are upper bounds only, and tightness is admittedly open (acknowledged in Sec. 7). The ε⁻⁴ term in Thm. 8 (from controlling the discretization error KL(P‖P→)) looks potentially loose relative to the ε⁻² rates in equilibrium methods (Ge et al., 2020), and no lower bound is provided even for the geometric interpolation AIS setting. Without tightness, the practical significance of the complexity result is uncertain.

The complexity is expressed in terms of the action A, which is generally not computable or controllable a priori for a given target. For arbitrary non-log-concave targets, the guarantee may be vacuous, and the paper provides lower bounds only for one specific one-dimensional Gaussian mixture instance (Prop. 9).

The RDS 'framework' in Sec. 6 / App. E.5 does not deliver a complete end-to-end complexity guarantee of its own: the KL(Q‖Q†) analysis is imported wholesale from prior works (Huang et al., 2024a,b; He et al., 2024; Vacher et al., 2025), whose guarantees are exponential in d or in 1/ε. Assembling these results is useful but limits the novelty and impact of this component.

Assumption 2 is somewhat restrictive and convenient: existence of a stationary point within distance O(1/√β) of the origin is imposed 'for technical purposes,' and the paper's claim of minimal assumptions on the target should be tempered accordingly (the analysis still requires β-smoothness and this stationarity condition).

The proof of Thm. 6 explicitly builds on Guo et al. (2025, Thm. 1) and Vargas et al. (2024, Prop. 3.3), and the JE/AIS identity framework is classical (Neal 2001; Jarzynski 1997; Crooks 1998). While the synthesis and the action-based analysis are new, the incremental technical novelty relative to these works should be more clearly delineated.

No numerical experiments whatsoever. Even for a theory paper, a small-scale empirical validation (e.g., verifying the predicted behavior on Gaussian mixtures where the action is computable) would strengthen the claims about the practical inefficiency of geometric interpolation vs. OU-based curves.

Minor presentation issues: typos ('poof methodology' on p.2), some notation burden (multiple path measures P, P→, P←, P^b→, P→), and occasional proof steps left informal (e.g., the Novikov condition is assumed throughout, per Remark 16).

strengths: Addresses a genuinely open problem: the first non-asymptotic (oracle) complexity analysis of annealed importance sampling and Jarzynski equality for normalizing constant estimation without requiring isoperimetric conditions (e.g., log-concavity or Poincaré) on the target distribution. Prior non-asymptotic results (Brosse et al. 2018; Ge et al. 2020; Andrieu et al. 2016) all rely on isoperimetry.

The proof strategy is elegant and technically substantive: bounding the relative-error probability via TV distance between forward and backward path measures, then controlling KL(P||P^→) and KL(P||P^←) via Girsanov's theorem and the W2 metric derivative/action from optimal transport (Lemmas 1, 5). The decomposition argument for AIS (Lemma 7, conditions (27)-(29)) connecting the number of annealing steps to the action is a real technical contribution, including an improved Θ(ε²) step size over Guo et al. (2025) (Remark 7).

The paper is not merely an upper-bound exercise: Proposition 1 gives an exponential lower bound on the action of geometric interpolation for a Gaussian mixture target, providing a quantitative explanation of the 'mass teleportation' phenomenon, and motivates the RDS-based algorithm. Theorem 6 (exponential gap between W1 and W2 metric derivatives on the same curve) is of independent mathematical interest.

Proposition 2 shows the OU-process curve has action at most dβ + m² under weak assumptions, cleanly motivating the reverse-diffusion-sampler-based algorithm, and Theorem 5 provides a framework connecting KL(Q||Q†) and TV(π, π_δ) to the accuracy criterion (1).

Useful extension results in the appendix: TI as a special case of AIS, and inference-time guarantees for PIS (Prop. 4) and CMCD (Prop. 5) relating training loss to estimator accuracy — results the original papers did not provide.

The writing is clear and well organized; the error criterion (1) is carefully motivated (median trick, equivalence with free-energy estimation, comparison to bias/variance in App. G); experiments on two multimodal targets with oracle-matched budgets show RDS-based estimators clearly outperform TI and geometric AIS, consistent with the theory.
weaknesses: The conceptual core (action-based analysis of annealed dynamics via Girsanov) is adapted from Guo et al. (2025), which the authors candidly acknowledge. The contribution is an adaptation to a different task plus a lower bound; this makes the novelty incremental rather than paradigm-shifting, though the extension to normalizing constant estimation is nontrivial (backward SDE arguments, discretization analysis).

The central bound depends on the action A of the interpolation curve, which is unknown a priori and not estimated; T = Θ(A/ε²) in Thm. 2 and the schedule in Thm. 4 require knowledge of A. Practical implementability of the theoretically optimal schedules is not discussed. The tightness of the upper bounds is unknown, and the ε⁻⁴ dependence is likely suboptimal (the authors admit this in the limitations).

Proposition 1's lower bound on the action does not directly imply exponential-time hardness for JE (the authors concede this), so the practical significance of the 'disadvantage of geometric interpolation' is suggestive rather than conclusive. Also, the W1 metric derivative gap (Thm. 6) is stated for a specific two-component mixture on R and its broader implications are not developed.

The RDS 'algorithm' is largely a recombination of existing samplers (RDMC, RSDMC, ZODMC, SNDMC) with the Jarzynski-type work functional; the resulting total complexities (App. E.5) inherit exponential-in-d or exponential-in-1/ε factors from the underlying methods, so the new framework does not yield an efficient algorithmic guarantee in the usual sense.

Experimental validation is limited to d = 2 (modified Müller-Brown and a 4-component Gaussian mixture). There are no experiments probing the theory itself (e.g., empirical scaling of error with T, M, or action), no higher-dimensional examples, and no comparison to closely related learned-sampler baselines (e.g., PIS, CMCD, sequential controlled Langevin diffusions), even though the paper derives guarantees for PIS/CMCD in the appendix.

Assumption 2 requires ∇V(0) = 0 with the justification that finding a stationary point is 'negligible cost'; for multimodal landscapes (the very setting motivating the paper) locating a relevant stationary point can be nontrivial, so this 'without loss of generality' step deserves more scrutiny.

In Lemma 6, condition (24) as stated (TV(π̂0, π0) ≲ 1) is nearly vacuous since TV ≤ 1; Remark 5 sharpens this to 2⁻⁵, but the main-text presentation could mislead. Similarly, several '≲ 1' constants in the accuracy bookkeeping hide constant-factor slack that matters for a 3/4-probability guarantee.

A formal lower bound (matching the upper bound, or at least for AIS in the discrete setting) is absent; the connection to the classical Jerrum-Valiant-Vazirani sampling/counting equivalence is made only informally.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuine and well-motivated gap: quantitative, non-asymptotic complexity guarantees for annealed importance sampling and Jarzynski-equality-based normalizing constant estimation, where prior work either assumed log-concavity/isoperimetry or was only asymptotic.

The action-based complexity framework is elegant and technically interesting. The use of Girsanov's theorem between forward/backward/path measures, the connection between the 'lag' in annealed Langevin dynamics and the W2 metric derivative, and the resulting bound T = O(A/ε^2) (Thm. 2) is a clean result that avoids explicit isoperimetric assumptions.

The exponential lower bound on the action of geometric interpolation (Prop. 1) for Gaussian mixture targets is a nice result, and the observed W1/W2 metric-derivative gap (Thm. 6 in appendix) is an independently interesting technical observation. It gives a quantitative account of 'mass teleportation'.

The placement of the results is thoughtful: the comparison with Guo et al. (2025) (sampling vs. normalizing constant estimation, continuous analogue of Jerrum et al. 1986) and the improved ε-dependence (Θ̃(ε^2) step size vs. Θ̃(ε^4)) are clearly articulated (Rmk. 7).

The paper is well organized and the proofs appear careful, with substantial technical machinery (backward stochastic integrals, Nelson's relation, discretization via exponential integrators) developed in the appendix.

Experiments on multimodal targets (modified Müller-Brown, Gaussian mixture) qualitatively support the central thesis that geometric-interpolation-based AIS fails on multimodality while reverse-diffusion-based estimators succeed.
weaknesses: Substantial overlap in proof technique with Guo et al. (2025). The authors themselves state that Thm. 2's proof 'builds on the techniques developed in Guo et al. (2025, Thm. 1)' and that Prop. 1's proof approach 'was used independently in Chemseddine et al. (2025)'. The core novelty is the transfer of an existing action-based framework from sampling to normalizing constant estimation, which is a natural rather than surprising extension. The claimed improvement in ε-dependence (ε^4 vs. ε^6) is a refinement, not a new method.

The central theoretical result (Thm. 2) holds only under idealized conditions: exact simulation of the SDE, known Z0, and exactly computable work functional. The practical algorithm (AIS, Thm. 4) inherits a dominant term of dβ^2 A^2/ε^4 whose tightness is unknown, and the paper concedes that the action's 'practical interpretability is not well understood'. Thus the theory-to-practice bridge is weak: the bounds do not clearly explain or predict when the proposed methods will work.

The RDS-based section (Sec. 5) is somewhat overstated as an algorithmic contribution. Thm. 5 only states sufficient conditions (KL(Q||Q†) ≲ ε^2, TV ≲ ε); the actual oracle complexities are imported directly from prior works (RDMC, RSDMC, ZODMC, SNDMC) and are all poor — exponential in various problem parameters (e.g., exp((β(m²∨d)/ε)^{O(d)}) for SNDMC, exp(β³ log³(...)) for RSDMC). No new algorithmic guarantee is actually derived for the proposed estimator beyond composing existing results with a TV-error argument.

Experimental evaluation is very limited: two 2-dimensional toy targets, no high-dimensional experiments, no comparison against strong learned-kernel alternatives (e.g., controlled Monte Carlo diffusion, sequential controlled Langevin, path integral samplers) that the paper itself discusses, and no empirical validation of the theory (e.g., verifying the predicted A/ε² scaling). The experiments demonstrate known failure modes of vanilla AIS rather than testing the paper's theoretical predictions.

Key limitations are acknowledged but unresolved: tightness of the upper bounds is unknown; the exponential action lower bound does not imply exponential runtime of JE; and the lower bound is established only for the specific geometric interpolation on a 1D two-component Gaussian mixture, leaving the generality of the 'geometric interpolation is bad' message open.

Significance is moderate: the work solidly extends an existing line of research to a related task, but the practical impact is limited by idealized assumptions, weak concrete guarantees for the proposed RDS-based estimator, and the acknowledged NP-hardness of the underlying problem class. For a 30% acceptance bar, the combination of incremental novelty and limited empirical grounding places it below the threshold.

strengths: Clear and meaningful theoretical contribution: the paper establishes the first non-asymptotic oracle complexity bound for AIS (Thm. 4) for estimating normalizing constants without requiring isoperimetric assumptions (e.g., log-concavity, Poincaré/LSI), a genuine gap in the literature compared to Brosse et al. (2018), Ge et al. (2020), and Andrieu et al. (2016).

Technically coherent proof framework: the use of forward/backward SDEs, Girsanov theorem (including a careful backward-integral version), Nelson's relation, and the Wasserstein metric derivative to connect the complexity to the 'action' of the interpolation curve is elegant and unifies JE, AIS, and RDS under one analysis.

The exponential lower bound on the action of geometric interpolation for Gaussian mixture targets (Prop. 1) is a novel, quantitative explanation of the 'mass teleportation' phenomenon, and is complemented by an interesting independent observation (Thm. 6) about the gap between W1 and W2 metric derivatives on the same curve.
The ε-dependence improvement over Guo et al. (2025) (Θ̃(ε²) vs Θ̃(ε⁴) step size, achieved by relaxing KL(P∥P→) ≲ 1 for the estimation task) is a concrete, well-argued technical contribution (Rmk. 7).

The paper is honest about limitations (unknown tightness of bounds, Prop. 1 not directly implying exponential runtime for JE, interpretability of the action), and the appendix is thorough and largely self-contained, including pseudo-code, TI-as-AIS connection, and new inference-time guarantees for PIS and CMCD (Props. 4-5).
weaknesses: The main complexity bounds (Thms. 2 and 4) depend on the action A, which is typically unknown a priori for the target distribution and cannot be easily estimated in practice; this significantly limits the practical applicability of the guarantees, which the authors acknowledge but do not resolve.

The empirical evaluation is narrow: only two 2-dimensional toy distributions (modified Müller-Brown and a 4-component Gaussian mixture). No higher-dimensional experiments, no validation of the theory's predicted complexity scalings (e.g., dependence on A, β, d, ε), and no comparison against other practical annealing methods (e.g., SMC, learned interpolations), which weakens the empirical claim of superiority over AIS.

The RDS-based alternative does not yield polynomial complexity in general: the transferred bounds (App. E.5) are exponential in d or ε (e.g., exp((β(m²∨d)/ε)^O(d)) for SNDMC), so the practical 'beyond isoperimetry' story is only a framework, not a polynomial-time algorithm.

Substantial overlap in proof techniques with Guo et al. (2025) (Girsanov-based discretization analysis, action-based bounds); while the target task (normalizing constants vs. sampling) is different and the backward SDE arguments add value, the conceptual novelty relative to that closest work is incremental.

Some technical conditions are assumed away (e.g., Novikov condition, uniqueness of Fokker-Planck solutions are merely assumed in footnotes), and the 3/4-probability relative-error criterion (1) is a relatively weak guarantee compared to bias/variance bounds, though the authors justify this choice in App. G.
Tightness of the upper bounds is unknown; no matching lower bounds for the general AIS setting are provided, so it is unclear whether the Õ(dβ²A²/ε⁴) dependence is optimal.
